blocks.text: Pregnancy is not a protective factor against psychosis or depression — it carries increased risk of suicide and mental health problems. Spontaneous major malformation occurs in 2–3% of all pregnancies; drugs account for only 5 of every 100 malformations.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Antenatal depression risk is 7–15% (around 10%), versus ~7% outside the perinatal period; relapse rate in those with a past history of depression is around 50% during pregnancy.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Postpartum depression carries a ~10% risk, can begin before delivery, and risk is higher with any previous depressive illness (irrespective of whether it was postpartum) and highest with bipolar illness.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: A significant depressive episode temporally related to childbirth occurs in 10–15% of women within 6 months postpartum, peaking at 3–4 weeks. Risk factors: personal/family history of depression, older age, single motherhood, poor relationship with own mother, ambivalent/unwanted pregnancy, poor social support, additional psychosocial stressors, severe baby blues, and previous postpartum psychosis.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Up to 75% of new mothers experience 'baby blues' — transient, mild mood and anxiety symptoms lasting up to two weeks that usually resolve spontaneously with no sequelae.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Delivery location (home vs hospital) is **NOT** associated with a difference in rates of blues or depression (Pop et al., 1995) — the genuine risk factors are child health problems, past depression, complicated antenatal course, and traumatic delivery.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: 'Delivery at home' is a deliberate distractor for postnatal depression risk factors — Pop et al. (1995) found no difference in blues/depression rates between home and hospital delivery, unlike the other genuine risk factors listed (traumatic delivery, complicated antenatal course, child health problems, past depression).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: The Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale is a 10-item screening tool covering depression, anxiety, anhedonia and self-harm/suicide dimensions; a score >16 specifically raises concern for suicidal ideation.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.subtopic: Postnatal depression screening (Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale)
blocks.note: Only appears in a single question's explanation, with no coverage in the book notes. Cross-check **EPDS** cut-off scores and their clinical implications against current **NICE** antenatal/postnatal mental health guidance.

sources.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Untreated postnatal depression risks attachment, behavioural and cognitive difficulties in the infant.

blocks.text: Risk of postpartum psychosis: 0.1–0.25% in the general population, 50% in bipolar disorder, and 50–90% in a woman with a prior episode of postpartum psychosis. Incidence overall is about 1 per 1000 births, and it is strongly linked to bipolar disorder.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Puerperal psychosis can present as mania, schizophreniform/acute polymorphic psychosis, or with confusion and disorientation. Recurrence rate is about 1 in 4 pregnancies, and there is a 20-fold increase in relative risk of psychosis in one's lifetime during the first postpartum month.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Risk of bipolar relapse is increased up to 8-fold in the first month postpartum, and most relapses are depressive; childbirth (with abortion and menstruation) is a recognised trigger of bipolar episodes.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: A prior episode of postpartum psychosis carries a 50–90% recurrence risk in a subsequent pregnancy — distinct from the 50% risk quoted for bipolar disorder generally and the 0.1–0.25% general-population risk.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Postpartum psychosis is most commonly associated with bipolar disorder — women with bipolar disorder have the highest risk of postpartum psychosis of any diagnostic group.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Postpartum psychosis typically has rapid onset within 2–4 weeks of childbirth and is a psychiatric emergency (risk of suicide and, rarely, infanticide), presenting with delusions, hallucinations, confusion/perplexity, severe mood swings, insomnia, agitation and rapid deterioration.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: In a woman with bipolar disorder who remains medication-free through pregnancy, relapse into depression after delivery is the most prevalent form of postpartum relapse overall — though bipolar I specifically carries a greater probability of postpartum psychosis/mania.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Even when a bipolar-disorder stem emphasises medication-free status while trying to conceive and evokes postpartum psychosis/mania, the statistically most likely tested outcome is relapse into depression after delivery — mania/psychosis are more dramatic, but depression is the most prevalent postpartum relapse type overall.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Disorders of the mother–infant relationship are prominent in 10–25% of women; harm from postpartum psychosis can range from neglect to infanticide.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

sections.title: 3. Pharmacological Treatment in Pregnancy — General Principles

blocks.text: Teratogenic risk is dose- and time-dependent; major malformations arise in the first trimester (organs at greatest risk during their fastest development — weeks 6–10 most vulnerable), while neonatal toxicity arises from third-trimester exposure.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: General principles: individualised risk–benefit analysis; monotherapy at the lowest effective dose; regular psychiatric and obstetric review; involve midwives, obstetricians and health visitors; avoid all drugs in the first trimester if possible; ensure adequate foetal screening; observe for neonatal withdrawal symptoms after birth.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Blood volume expands by ~30% by the third trimester, so dose increases are frequently required as pregnancy advances.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **NICE** (2020 update) identifies weeks 2–14 as the most sensitive period for foetal malformation on teratogen exposure.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: The 'most sensitive period for foetal malformation' is tested in the question bank as weeks 2–14 (citing **NICE** 2020) — a wider window than the **SPMM** book's 'weeks 6–10 most vulnerable' framing. Go with whichever framing the stem's cited guideline points to.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Schizophrenia in pregnancy: consensus is to use an antipsychotic at every stage of pregnancy, particularly for patients with a history of frequent relapse. Most experience is with **chlorpromazine**, **trifluoperazine**, **haloperidol**, **olanzapine** and **clozapine**.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **Olanzapine** is the antipsychotic most widely used by **UK** perinatal services for schizophrenia in pregnancy.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: 'Widely used by **UK** perinatal services for schizophrenia in pregnancy' is tested specifically as **olanzapine**, not **amisulpride**, **quetiapine**, **risperidone** or **aripiprazole**, despite all being plausible atypical antipsychotic options.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Depression in pregnancy: consider delaying treatment to the 2nd/3rd trimester, or psychological treatment (e.g. **CBT**) first; moderate/severe depression should be treated with an antidepressant if psychological management fails or is unavailable. Recommended antidepressants: **nortriptyline**, **amitriptyline**, **imipramine**, **fluoxetine** — avoid **paroxetine**.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Bipolar disorder in pregnancy: patients with severe illness or high relapse risk should generally continue medication; avoid **valproate** and combinations of mood stabilisers. If **valproate** or **carbamazepine** is used, give prophylactic folic acid 5mg/day from at least 1 month pre-conception, and prophylactic vitamin K to mother and neonate after delivery.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: TCAs cause no significant malformation in any trimester; **nortriptyline** and desipramine are preferred (less hypotensive/anticholinergic). High-dose third-trimester use can cause reversible neonatal withdrawal (irritability, feeding/sleep difficulty, convulsions).

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: SSRIs show no increase in major malformation (exception: **paroxetine**); however there is a 13.3% increase in spontaneous abortion (also seen with **mirtazapine**/**bupropion**), ~1 week reduction in gestational age, and ~175g lower mean birth weight.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **Paroxetine** (especially high-dose first-trimester exposure) is linked to cardiac malformation (**VSD**, **ASD**); third-trimester use risks abrupt neonatal withdrawal. **Fluoxetine** has the most evidence and appears safer; **sertraline** has the least placental exposure. Late-pregnancy **SSRI** exposure carries a small absolute increased risk of persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn. Neonatal withdrawal risk is highest with **paroxetine** and **venlafaxine** due to their short half-lives.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: MAOIs have very limited safety evidence; avoid due to hypertensive crisis risk and suspected increased congenital malformation risk — switch to a safer antidepressant instead.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Pregnant women who stop taking antidepressants are about 5 times more likely to relapse into depression than those who continue — a relative-risk figure distinct from the absolute relapse-rate figures below.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: SSRIs are **NOT** associated with neural tube defects — the tested **SSRI**-associated effects are neonatal irritability, spontaneous abortion, premature birth and reduced birth weight; neural tube defects are a **valproate** association, not an **SSRI** one.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Neural tube defects are **NOT** an **SSRI** risk in pregnancy — that is a **valproate** association. The tested **SSRI** risks are neonatal irritability, spontaneous abortion, prematurity and reduced birth weight.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: In psychiatric-setting cohorts, women with recurrent depression who discontinue antidepressant medication show relapse rates up to 70%; in obstetric-setting cohorts (likely milder depression), relapse risk is similar whether or not medication is continued. Risk is highest for those with severe and/or recurrent depression.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Around 40% of pregnancies in women with a history of recurrent major depression result in relapse — a figure distinct from, and not to be confused with, the 70% relapse-on-discontinuation figure above.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Three different antidepressant/relapse statistics are tested for this topic and are easy to conflate: a 5-fold relative risk of relapse on stopping antidepressants generally, a 70% relapse rate specifically in psychiatric-setting cohorts with recurrent depression who discontinue medication, and a 40% relapse rate in pregnancies of women with recurrent major depression more generally — check exactly what population/exposure the stem specifies before picking a number.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Continuing **lithium** through the first trimester carries roughly a 1 in 10 chance of malformation. **UK** National Teratology Information Service data suggest a ~3-fold increased risk of malformation overall, weighted toward an ~8-fold increase in cardiac malformation (Williams & Oke, 2000).

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Ebstein's anomaly: relative risk is 10–20x the general population, but absolute risk remains low (~1:1000); general-population baseline risk is 1:20,000 (Cohen et al., **JAMA** 1994). Maximum risk window is 2–6 weeks post-conception, when many pregnancies are still undiscovered.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: 9.5 is given as the 'closest' tested value among discrete options for the relative risk of Ebstein's anomaly with **lithium** exposure.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: The Ebstein's anomaly relative-risk question accepts 9.5 as the 'closest' answer among discrete options — a rare explicit acknowledgement in the explanation that the true evidence range (10–20x) doesn't match any listed option exactly.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: The general-population prevalence of Ebstein's anomaly is 1 in 20,000; more recent data suggest the **lithium**-associated risk magnitude is smaller than previously estimated.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.forTopic: Lithium and Ebstein's anomaly — the key numbers
expansion: 3-fold — overall relative risk of malformation with 1st-trimester **lithium**
8-fold — relative risk weighting toward cardiac malformation
10-20-fold — relative risk of Ebstein's anomaly specifically
1:1000 — absolute risk of Ebstein's anomaly with **lithium** exposure
1:20,000 — general-population baseline risk of Ebstein's anomaly

blocks.text: Foetal **lithium** toxicity — hypotonia, lethargy, poor reflexes, respiratory difficulty, cardiac arrhythmias — is reversible and does not cause later complications. Risk of relapse after stopping **lithium** is up to 70% within 6 months (faster discontinuation = higher risk), and is threefold higher in the puerperium for women with bipolar disorder who elect to stop, compared with non-pregnant, non-puerperal women.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Risk to mother and child of **lithium** withdrawal may have been underestimated, while risk to the foetus of **lithium** exposure may have been overestimated.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Screening for Ebstein's anomaly: level 2 ultrasound and foetal echocardiography at 6 and 18 weeks' gestation (Maudsley, 2007) — not at 20–24 weeks, a commonly confused distractor.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Ebstein's anomaly screening timing is tested as exactly 6 and 18 weeks' gestation (Maudsley 2007) — options like '20 and 24 weeks' or '2 and 10 weeks' are deliberate distractors.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Third-trimester **lithium** dose requirements increase as total body water rises, but requirement drops abruptly back to pre-pregnancy levels immediately after delivery.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.title: Lithium management in pregnancy (Kohen 2004 / Maudsley 2007)
rows: Serum **lithium** level monitored every 4 weeks throughout pregnancy
Adjust to the lower end of the therapeutic range
Should not be discontinued abruptly; taper to 60–70% of maintenance dose before delivery
Use lower doses with frequent blood monitoring
Can help reduce the risk of puerperal psychosis
Level 2 ultrasound and echocardiography at 6 and 18 weeks' gestation to screen for Ebstein's anomaly
Increased dose often required as total body water increases; requirement returns abruptly to pre-pregnancy level immediately after delivery

blocks.title: Teratogenic risk figures — lithium, valproate, carbamazepine, lamotrigine
rows: **RR** 10–20x general population; absolute risk ~1:1000; general-population baseline 1:20,000
Two different editions give two different overall figures
Distinct from the 'any malformation' figure above

question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Sodium **valproate** is the most teratogenic mood stabiliser: overall birth-defect risk is quoted as 7.2% by Maudsley/**NICE** (comparable to the **UK** epilepsy & pregnancy registry; the North American registry quotes ~10%). Risk is dose-related, mostly manifests 17–30 days post-conception, and increases with family history of neural tube defects.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: A more recent figure (Maudsley 14th ed., 2021): **valproate** confers around a 1 in 10 (~10%) risk of major malformation if taken throughout pregnancy — **valproate** should not be used in women of childbearing age except when all other treatment has failed.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Valproate**-specific congenital anomalies: neural tube defects (1–2%, ~10-fold increase in spina bifida), digital/limb defects, heart defects (**VSD**, pulmonary stenosis — 4-fold increase), urogenital malformations, low birth weight, psychomotor slowing, foetal distress, growth retardation and hepatotoxicity.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: A **BAP** (2017) figure gives the spina bifida risk specifically as around 1 in 100 (~13-fold increase from ~0.09% baseline to 1–2% with **valproate**) — note this neural-tube-defect-specific figure differs from the overall malformation figure (1 in 10) above; the two are easily conflated.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Valproate**'s overall major-malformation risk (~1 in 10, Maudsley 14th ed.) and its neural-tube-defect-specific risk (~1 in 100, **BAP** 2017) are two different, easily-confused figures tested separately — read carefully whether the stem asks about 'any malformation' or 'neural tube defect/spina bifida' specifically.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Valproate** exposure is linked to lower verbal **IQ**: 42% of children exposed to **valproate** monotherapy in utero had verbal **IQ** <80 (22% <70; Adab et al., 2004); 30% needed special educational support vs 3–6% with other antiepileptic monotherapy (Breen & Davenport, 2006). The confounding effect of maternal seizures on **IQ** is not fully known.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Verbal **IQ** is the neurocognitive domain most affected by in-utero **valproate** exposure (Adab et al., 2004).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Carbamazepine**: 0.5–1% risk of spina bifida, craniofacial anomalies, growth retardation and reduced head circumference; in one exposed cohort, craniofacial defects occurred in 11%, fingernail hypoplasia in 26%, and developmental delay in 20%. Mechanistic overlap with foetal hydantoin syndrome is proposed via a shared arene oxide metabolic pathway.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: A Maudsley 14th ed. (2021)/**BAP** (2017) figure: **carbamazepine** roughly doubles overall malformation risk (~2% to ~3.5–5%) and gives an ~3-fold increase in spina bifida risk specifically (from ~0.09% general-population baseline to ~0.3–0.5%) — this numerically differs from the book's 0.5–1% figure above.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Carbamazepine**'s spina bifida risk is tested as 0.3–0.5% (Maudsley 14th ed.) — don't substitute **valproate**'s much higher neural-tube-defect figures (1–2%/1 in 100) for **carbamazepine**; the two drugs have different, drug-specific numbers.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: If **carbamazepine** is used in pregnancy, prophylactic vitamin K should be given to both mother and neonate after delivery.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Lamotrigine** may be associated with cleft palate; **lamotrigine** monotherapy carries a 3.2% frequency of malformations.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Conventional antipsychotics carry low teratogenic risk overall and are comparatively safe (California Child Health Development Project, ~19,000 births); low-potency agents are linked to transient perinatal syndrome/floppy infant/withdrawal symptoms, and first-trimester low-potency use carries a small but statistically significant increased malformation risk (2–2.4%). First-trimester **haloperidol** has been linked to limb deformities in one study, not confirmed by others (Yaeger et al., 2006).

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Atypical antipsychotics (**clozapine**, **olanzapine**, **risperidone**, **quetiapine**) show no serious newborn effects in case reports; **clozapine** carries specific concerns (no foetal white cell monitoring, agranulocytosis/hypotension risk, reports of stillbirth and neonatal seizure). Gestational diabetes can occur with **clozapine**/**olanzapine**. Data on **aripiprazole** are limited, with no case reports for other SGAs.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Anticholinergic drugs (in combination with antipsychotics) carry reported teratogenicity — avoid, or use the lowest possible dose if needed.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.forTopic: Drugs to specifically avoid (or use with most caution) in pregnancy
expansion: **Valproate** — most teratogenic mood stabiliser, avoid in women of childbearing age if possible
Anticholinergics — reported teratogenicity, avoid or use lowest dose
MAOIs — hypertensive crisis risk, suspected malformation risk, switch to a safer antidepressant
**Paroxetine** — high-dose 1st-trimester cardiac malformation risk (**VSD**/**ASD**), 3rd-trimester withdrawal risk

blocks.text: Benzodiazepines: first-trimester exposure carries a 0.6% risk of oral cleft plus **CNS**/urinary tract malformation; other risks include neonatal withdrawal, respiratory depression, and floppy baby syndrome (muscular hypotonia) — best avoided in pregnancy. **Zopiclone** shows no animal teratogenicity but human data are lacking.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **Clonazepam** in pregnancy is most associated with neonatal hypotonia ('floppy baby syndrome') from third-trimester exposure — not Ebstein's anomaly, **VSD** or persistent pulmonary hypertension (associated with **lithium** and SSRIs respectively). First-trimester oral cleft association has not been consistently confirmed in later studies.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Clonazepam** in pregnancy is tested as causing neonatal hypotonia ('floppy baby', 3rd-trimester exposure) — not Ebstein's anomaly, **VSD**, or persistent pulmonary hypertension, which are the tested associations for **lithium** and SSRIs respectively.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **ECT** has relatively few side effects and fewer risks than untreated mood episodes or pharmacotherapy in pregnancy. Occasional congenital malformation reports do not implicate **ECT** causally, and complications during pregnancy are uncommon and transient.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Anaesthetic considerations: barbiturates/atropine can reduce foetal heart-rate beat-to-beat variability, and atropine can cause foetal tachycardia; uterine smooth muscle does not routinely contract during a seizure, so premature labour is almost unheard of; seizure threshold is decreased by oestrogen and increased by progesterone; prolonged gastric emptying time in pregnancy raises the risk of gastric regurgitation and aspiration pneumonitis (Yonkers et al., 2004).

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: When considering **ECT** in a pregnant woman, delayed gastric emptying (raising aspiration risk) is the most relevant physiological change for anaesthetic planning — not decreased protein binding, increased renal clearance, or increased seizure threshold.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: For **ECT** in pregnancy, the tested 'most relevant factor' is delayed gastric emptying (aspiration risk) — not decreased protein binding, increased renal clearance, or increased seizure threshold, even though these other physiological changes of pregnancy are real.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Evidence is based on small case series/single case reports; all psychotropics are excreted in breast milk. Treat maternal illness as a priority, use monotherapy at the lowest effective dose, and take medication after (not before) breastfeeding to avoid peak drug levels in milk.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: The infant plasma concentration threshold conventionally regarded as low-risk/'safe' is 10% of the maternal therapeutic dose; a breast milk/maternal plasma ratio >1 suggests a high likelihood of infant drug exposure.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Pre-term/immature infants should not be exposed to psychotropics (immature liver function, greater sensitivity); infants over 10 weeks old are at lower risk if there is no evidence of drug accumulation. Infant cardiac, renal and hepatic function should be checked before breastfeeding, and infant progress/adverse effects (drowsiness, hypotonia, rigidity, tremor, withdrawal) monitored throughout.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Maudsley (2007) drug-of-choice recommendations for breastfeeding: antidepressant — **paroxetine** or **sertraline**; antipsychotic — **sulpiride** or **olanzapine**; mood stabiliser — avoid if possible, **valproate** if essential; sedatives — **lorazepam** for anxiety, **zolpidem** for sleep.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

sources.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf
question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf
question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: SSRIs and TCAs (except **doxepin**) are probably safe in breastfeeding with low infant serum levels; preferred TCAs are **amitriptyline** and **imipramine** (maternal plasma and breast-milk concentrations are similar). N-desmethyldoxepin (**doxepin**'s long-acting metabolite) may accumulate and cause drowsiness/respiratory depression in the infant; **clomipramine** plasma levels in breastfed infants have been reported high.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **Sertraline** is first-line in the **USA** with the largest study samples; **paroxetine** has a lower milk/plasma ratio than **fluoxetine** and **sertraline**. **Fluoxetine**/norfluoxetine appear in breast milk but not reliably in infant plasma; rare case reports describe irritability, cyanosis, somnolence with higher doses, without confirmed cognitive/neurological effects. MAOIs should be stopped before breastfeeding (no published safety data).

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **Sertraline** has the most favourable evidence base among antidepressants for breastfeeding, given a lower risk of side effects/withdrawal than **paroxetine** and undetectable/low infant plasma concentrations.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: SSRIs as a class are preferred for breastfeeding; SNRIs and **mirtazapine** also show minimal milk passage; **bupropion** is avoided where possible (case reports of infant seizure); TCAs pass more into milk than SSRIs and are avoided where possible, with **doxepin** considered contraindicated.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: High-potency conventional antipsychotics (**haloperidol**, **chlorpromazine**, **perphenazine**) are preferred during breastfeeding (less sedation/autonomic effect) and considered safe; delayed development has been reported in 3 infants exposed to a combination of **haloperidol** and **chlorpromazine**.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Among atypicals, **sulpiride**, **olanzapine** and **risperidone** have limited data suggesting safety in breastfeeding; no published data exist for **aripiprazole**, **amisulpride**, sertindole or **ziprasidone**. **Clozapine** is contraindicated (accumulates in breast milk/foetal serum due to higher foetal albumin concentration) — reported effects include agranulocytosis (spontaneously reversible), decreased sucking reflex, drowsiness, seizure, irritability and cardiovascular instability.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **Lithium** is contraindicated in breastfeeding per Kohen (2005), though Maudsley (2007) frames it as ranging from absolute contraindication to maternal informed choice. 40–50% of maternal serum level is excreted in milk; infant serum can reach up to 200% of maternal level (diminished neonatal renal clearance); toxicity (cyanosis, lethargy, hypotonia, heart murmur) resolves after stopping breastfeeding.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **Valproate** infant serum levels range from undetectable to 40%; reported adverse effects (thrombocytopenia, anaemia) resolve after stopping breastfeeding.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Sodium **valproate** is the most likely cause of breastfed-infant thrombocytopenia and anaemia that resolves on stopping breastfeeding — distinguishing it from **carbamazepine**, **lithium** and **lamotrigine**, which have different characteristic adverse-effect profiles.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Carbamazepine** infant serum range is 5–65%; reported effects include cholestatic hepatitis, transient hepatic dysfunction, seizure-like activity, irritability, high-pitched crying, hyperexcitability and poor feeding. **Lamotrigine** infant serum range is ~30% of maternal concentration with no adverse effects noted.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: Benzodiazepines should ideally be stopped before pregnancy; long-acting agents can cause infant lethargy/poor suckling/weight loss, and persistent apnoea has been reported with **clonazepam**. **Diazepam** and **alprazolam** should be avoided; low-dose short-acting agents (**temazepam**, **oxazepam**) are mostly safe. **Buspirone**, zaleplon and **zopiclone** should be avoided; **zolpidem** is considered safe.

source.file: books/7-2-perinatal-psychiatry.pdf

blocks.text: **Clonazepam** is the psychotropic **NOT** recommended for initiation during breastfeeding among typical exam options (**sertraline**, **lorazepam**, **mirtazapine**, **olanzapine** all considered reasonable) — reflecting a preference for short-acting benzodiazepines like **lorazepam** over long-acting ones like **clonazepam**.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Among breastfeeding sedative/hypnotic options, **clonazepam** (long half-life) is the one **NOT** recommended for initiation, in contrast to **lorazepam** (short half-life) which is considered acceptable — the exam tests this half-life-driven distinction rather than a blanket 'avoid all benzodiazepines' rule.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **Zolpidem** is the safe sedative choice for breastfeeding insomnia without depressive features; zaleplon and **zopiclone** are excreted in breast milk and should be avoided.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

expansion: **Lithium** — contraindicated (40–50% of maternal serum level excreted in milk)

blocks.text: About 85% of women experience at least one mild premenstrual symptom; 20–25% experience moderate–severe premenstrual syndrome (**PMS**). **PMDD** (now included in **DSM-5** and **ICD-11**) occurs in 2–8% of women with regular menstrual cycles.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **PMS** symptoms peak 2 days before menses and last from a few days to 2 weeks; the most severe and earliest symptoms are anger and irritability. Severe **PMS** affects 3–8% of women of reproductive age; comorbidity with mood disorder occurs in 30–70%; **PMS** raises the risk of both premenstrual depression and postnatal depression.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: **DSM-5** **PMDD** requires at least 5 symptoms including at least one 'core' symptom: marked affective lability, irritability, depressed mood, or anxiety. Other possible symptoms include decreased interest in usual activities, concentration difficulty, low energy, sleep/appetite changes, feeling overwhelmed/out of control, and physical symptoms. 'Feelings of guilt' is not a listed **DSM-5** **PMDD** symptom.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: 'Feelings of guilt' is the deliberate non-**DSM-5** **PMDD** symptom distractor — the four core **PMDD** symptoms are affective lability, irritability, depressed mood and anxiety (at least one required), alongside decreased interest, concentration difficulty, low energy, sleep/appetite change, and feeling overwhelmed.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

expansion: Anxiety — at least one of these four required, alongside other symptoms, for ≥5 total symptoms

blocks.text: Serotonin is the neurotransmitter most implicated aetiologically in **PMS**/**PMDD**: reduced luteal-phase whole-blood serotonin, reduced platelet serotonin/**imipramine** binding, exacerbation of symptoms after tryptophan depletion, and blunted neuroendocrine responses to serotonergic probes (e.g. m-chlorophenylpiperazine).

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: SSRIs are first-line for severe **PMS**/**PMDD**; **fluoxetine** is the most studied agent and has the largest evidence base.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: 'Largest evidence base for severe **PMS**/**PMDD**' is tested as **fluoxetine**, not **citalopram** — **PMDD** trial evidence specifically favours **fluoxetine** even though SSRIs are often treated as interchangeable elsewhere.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Evidence-based **PMDD** antidepressant options include **fluoxetine**, **sertraline**, **paroxetine**, **citalopram**, **escitalopram**, **venlafaxine** and **clomipramine**; **reboxetine** lacks evidence for this indication.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: SSRIs for **PMDD** can be dosed continuously or intermittently (e.g. from ovulation to menses, or on symptomatic days only) — intermittent use does not require pre-existing clinical depression to be effective.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Intermittent **SSRI** dosing for **PMDD** is well tolerated and not associated with significant discontinuation symptoms, but may be less effective than continuous dosing specifically for premenstrual physical symptoms.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

blocks.text: Intermittent **SSRI** dosing for **PMDD** is **NOT** poorly tolerated and does **NOT** cause significant discontinuation symptoms — the correct 'true' statement tested is that it is specifically less effective for physical (not mood) symptoms compared with continuous dosing.

source.file: question_bank/Clinical Parts_ Paper B/MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf

Verify current treatment recommendations against the Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines (15th ed.) and current **NICE** guidance before relying on this section alone.

blocks.subtopic: Version discrepancies in teratogenic risk figures
blocks.note: The **SPMM** book notes cite the 9th-edition (2007) Maudsley Guidelines and older **NICE**/registry data for **valproate**/**carbamazepine**/**lithium** risk figures, while several question-bank explanations cite the 14th-edition (2021) Maudsley Guidelines and **BAP** (2017) consensus guidance with different numeric figures for the same drugs (e.g. **valproate** malformation risk quoted as 7.2% in the book vs ~10% in a question). Both are reproduced above with their respective sources rather than reconciled into one number — verify current figures against the Maudsley Prescribing Guidelines (15th ed.) before quoting a single value in the exam.

The question bank file for this topic (MCQs Perinatal Psychiatry_ Attempt review.pdf) contains only **SBA**-format items — no dedicated **EMI** file exists for perinatal psychiatry in the manifest, so all examiner traps above are tagged **SBA**. If **EMI**-style perinatal content exists elsewhere (e.g. embedded within a general Adult or Forensic **EMI** file), it was not reviewed here.
